title: Hidden Third Planet Found Orbiting Beta Pictoris in Decade-Long Cosmic Hide and Seek
excerpt: Two independent teams using ground-based and space telescopes simultaneously discovered Beta Pictoris d, a gas giant 2.4 times Jupiter's mass that had been lurking undetected in archival data for over a decade.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Beta Pictoris d, a gas giant, was discovered by two teams using different telescopes.
  • It is the faintest exoplanet directly imaged, 100 times fainter than Beta Pictoris b.
  • The planet has a 91-year orbit and an atmosphere rich in carbon compounds.
  • Next-gen telescopes may reveal additional rocky planets in the Beta Pictoris system.
Discovering Beta Pictoris d
›Discovered by two teams simultaneously using different telescopes.
›Utilized Chile's Very Large Telescope and NASA's James Webb Space Telescope.
›Research published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
›Discovery involved analyzing 11 years of archival data.
  • Two independent research teams discovered Beta Pictoris d simultaneously — one using Chile's Very Large Telescope, the other using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope.
  • The new planet is the faintest exoplanet ever directly imaged from Earth, 100 times fainter than its sibling Beta Pictoris b, with a mass about 2.4 times Jupiter.
  • Beta Pictoris d has a 91-year orbit and an atmosphere rich in carbon dioxide, methane, carbon monoxide, and water.
  • Next-generation telescopes like ESO's Extremely Large Telescope, expected online in 2029, may reveal rocky planets hiding in the same system.

A gas giant that spent more than a decade hiding in plain sight has been unmasked 63 light-years from Earth, making the Beta Pictoris system only the second known multi-planet system with more than two planets captured through direct imaging.

Beta Pictoris d was discovered simultaneously by two independent teams whose findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. One group, led by Ben Sutlieff of the University of Edinburgh and Markus Bonse of the European Southern Observatory (ESO), used the ERIS instrument on Chile's Very Large Telescope. The other, led by Aidan Gibbs of the University of California and Jean-Baptiste Ruffio, detected the planet using JWST's NIRSpec integral field unit.

A Serendipitous Discovery

Sutlieff was not searching for a new planet. In December 2025, he was using the VLT to study the atmosphere of Beta Pictoris b, one of the first exoplanets ever directly imaged. A faint speck in his data caught his attention.

"Normally, when you see things like that, you work on the data some more, and these little scrappy signals go away because they're not real. They're noise and they vanish."

- Ben Sutlieff, University of Edinburgh

He handed the observations to Bonse, who applied machine learning algorithms to clean the images. The signal persisted. To confirm the object was genuinely orbiting Beta Pictoris, the team combed through archival imagery spanning 11 years from both the VLT and JWST. The planet had been there all along, concealed by the glare of its much brighter siblings — the researchers titled their paper a "decade-long game of hide-and-seek."

A Record-Setting Gas Giant

Beta Pictoris d is the faintest exoplanet ever directly imaged from the ground — 100 times fainter than Beta Pictoris b. With an estimated mass of 2.4 times Jupiter, it is light compared to the system's other two planets, both roughly 10 times Jupiter's mass.

The planet orbits its host star — nearly twice the mass of our Sun — every 91 years. Most known gas giant exoplanets complete their circuits in days or weeks. Its orbit at roughly 26 astronomical units from the star appears consistent with sculpting the inner edge of Beta Pictoris's famous debris disk.

Gibbs's team using JWST captured the planet's atmospheric spectrum, revealing absorption features from methane, carbon monoxide, and water. The planet's red color points to strong carbon dioxide absorption. Its estimated temperature sits around 600 Kelvin (327°C).

Why This System Matters

Beta Pictoris holds a special place in astronomy. It was the first star system where a circumstellar debris disk was directly imaged, and Beta Pictoris b was among the first exoplanets ever photographed. The system, only about 20 million years old, offers a window into planetary formation in its early stages.

With three confirmed planets now visible through direct imaging, it joins HR 8799 as only the second such multi-planet system — providing rare opportunities to compare planets that formed from the same material at roughly the same time.

"If they formed in the same system, they formed from the same material; they're all roughly the same age," Sutlieff told IFLScience. "This really lets us understand how the way that these planets form and where they form can have an impact on what they end up being like in their later life."

What Comes Next

ESO's Extremely Large Telescope, expected to begin operations in 2029, and the Giant Magellan Telescope will push direct imaging further — potentially down to rocky worlds.

"I would not be at all surprised if there are rocky planets in Beta Pictoris. With ELT, the Giant Magellan Telescope, maybe we're going to be able to start detecting those as well!"

- Ben Sutlieff, University of Edinburgh

Bonse noted that ground-based telescopes cost roughly 30 times less to operate than JWST, allowing astronomers to cast a wider net. The Gibbs team's work also set a precedent: Beta Pictoris d is the first planet discovered using spectral template matching with moderate-resolution spectroscopy, a technique that could unlock detection of more hidden worlds buried within bright debris disks across the galaxy.
